sources.title: DOE Releases New Report Evaluating Increase in Electricity Demand from Data Centers
sources.evidence_locator: Article body paragraphs reporting 2023 electricity share, 2028 range, and DOE power-system response
sources.evidence_summary: DOE reports that U.S. data centers used about 4.4% of electricity in 2023 and could reach roughly 6.7%-12% by 2028. It frames the response across generation, storage, transmission expansion, and demand flexibility.
sources.limitations: This is an official summary of the LBNL report, not the underlying full report; it supports demand and system-level constraints but not node-level value capture or China localization conclusions.
sources.notes: Accepted as public official evidence for demand growth and system-level power constraints.

sources.title: 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report
sources.evidence_locator: DOE-linked original PDF; local retrieval redirected to an access challenge
sources.evidence_summary: The DOE page attributes the public demand figures to this LBNL report, but the report body was not available for excerpt-level review in the current environment.
sources.limitations: Do not treat as accepted S0 evidence until the PDF body, methodology, and tables are reviewed directly.
sources.notes: Preserved as the preferred original source for later full-text acquisition.

sources.title: Powering the AI Revolution
sources.evidence_locator: Key takeaways and section 'What infrastructure powers the AI revolution?'
sources.evidence_summary: J.P. Morgan states that AI compute depends on data centers and reliable power, that AI is increasing infrastructure demand, and that grid capacity is a key development constraint.
sources.limitations: This is institutional analysis and interview material, not a power-system dataset. It supports the research framing, not precise market sizing or company conclusions.
sources.notes: Accepted for the demand-to-grid-capacity causal framing.

sources.title: Grid Resilience: Neglected No More
sources.evidence_locator: Key takeaways, grid investment discussion, and permitting/lead-time section
sources.evidence_summary: The article links data-center demand with aging grid infrastructure, expects grid buildout and upgrades, and highlights multi-year transmission development constraints.
sources.limitations: Forecasts and investment estimates are J.P. Morgan analysis with cited third-party inputs. They do not prove which equipment category captures superior margins or localized scarcity.
sources.notes: Accepted for grid buildout and interconnection bottleneck context.

sources.title: The data center surge: Building the backbone of the digital age
sources.author: Fahmi Enam and Scott Wilcoxen
sources.evidence_locator: Public transcript paragraphs on data-center power draw, AI workload buildout, and power capacity
sources.evidence_summary: The transcript describes data-center capacity in power terms, a shift toward AI workloads, high capital intensity, and power capacity as a constrained input to new builds.
sources.limitations: The transcript contains expert estimates and commercial-banking observations. It is not engineering validation of a specific rack architecture or proof of equipment profitability.
sources.notes: Accepted as attributable institutional commentary with a public transcript.

sources.title: NVIDIA GB200 NVL72
sources.evidence_locator: Product overview and energy-efficient infrastructure sections
sources.evidence_summary: NVIDIA describes GB200 NVL72 as a rack-scale system with 72 GPUs and liquid cooling, and says liquid cooling enables greater compute density and reduced floor-space use.
sources.limitations: Vendor product material is reliable for the product architecture it describes, but vendor performance comparisons do not establish industry-wide economics or supplier value capture.
sources.notes: Accepted for rack-scale and liquid-cooling architecture only.

sources.title: NVIDIA 800 VDC Architecture
sources.evidence_locator: Sections 'Powering AI Factories With 800 VDC', 'Moving to an 800 VDC Architecture', and 'The Advantages of 800 VDC Technology'
sources.evidence_summary: NVIDIA presents 800 VDC as a future power-distribution route intended to reduce conversion stages, current, copper use, cable bulk, and distribution losses while supporting denser AI racks.
sources.limitations: This is a vendor roadmap and architecture proposal. It validates the technical direction described by NVIDIA, not adoption timing, market share, margins, or listed-company exposure.
sources.notes: Accepted for technical-route review and for challenging blanket copper/equipment beneficiary claims.

sources.title: Building the 800 VDC Ecosystem for Efficient, Scalable AI Factories
sources.author: Neeraj Srivastava
sources.evidence_locator: Rack power-density discussion, 'Advantages of 800 VDC', and '800 VDC power distribution in next-generation AI factories'
sources.evidence_summary: The technical article describes rack power density moving beyond 100 kW, workload volatility affecting grid interconnection, and an 800 VDC route that reduces copper and conversion layers. It also describes a future architecture that can remove some AC switchgear, transformer, UPS, and PDU stages from the data hall.
sources.limitations: The author represents NVIDIA and discusses a proposed ecosystem. Technical statements are useful for route analysis, while commercial adoption, bill-of-materials allocation, and profit pools require independent evidence.
sources.notes: Accepted as vendor-authored technical evidence, with explicit commercial limitations.
